payload.name: Extract Individual Attributes from Enumerated Group Lists
payload.description: When a user assigns distinct traits to each member of a group (e.g., pets, family) in one message, during extraction.
content: During extraction, if a message assigns specific attributes to each member of an enumerated group (e.g., 'oldest is relaxed, second is playful...'), create a candidate for each member-attribute pair, not only a general summary.
Record the member identifier (e.g., oldest, youngest, named pet) and its stated attribute(s) in a durable memory (state or relationship), with the speaker as subject.
Keep the general affectionate or relational framing in a separate candidate if present, but do not let it substitute for the specific per-member facts.
Stop after one candidate per distinct member-attribute statement; do not infer attributes not explicitly stated.

candidates.solves: Construction extraction sometimes collapses a user's explicit enumeration of distinct traits for multiple group members into a single general sentiment memory, losing the individual facts needed to answer later questions. This Skill ensures each enumerated attribute pair is captured.

payload.name: Extract Factual Answers as State Memories
payload.description: When a speaker directly answers a question about a pet, person, or possession with concrete factual details, create a state memory during extraction even without emotional or preference language.
content: During extraction, treat direct factual answers (e.g., what a pet eats, a person's role, an item's condition) as state memory candidates even when the message contains no preference or emotion words.
Attribute the fact to the specific subject named and preserve the exact details stated; do not wait for repetition or a like/dislike framing.
Stop after capturing the explicit facts in the answer; do not infer additional attributes.

candidates.solves: Construction extraction sometimes skips concrete factual statements about a user's pets, possessions, or people when the message is casual or directly answers a question, because no preference or emotional cue triggers candidate generation. This skill ensures explicit factual answers are captured as durable state memories.

payload.name: Preserve Explicit Evaluative Words in Extracted Memories
payload.description: During extraction, when a memory candidate's source statement contains an explicit adjective or evaluative phrase describing a person, group, bond, event, or experience, preserve that exact wording in the memory content.
content: During extraction, if the speaker uses an explicit evaluative adjective or phrase (e.g., 'awesome', 'great', 'terrible', 'the best part'), include that exact wording in the memory content; do not replace it with a broader paraphrase like 'strong bonds' or 'positive experience'.
When a later message elaborates on the same statement, update the existing memory to add the explicit descriptor rather than creating a new candidate or leaving the paraphrase unchanged.
Keep the memory compact: capture the relationship or entity and the exact evaluative term(s) in one memory; do not enumerate synonyms or expand into unrelated details.
Apply only to explicit first-person descriptions; do not infer evaluative words that the speaker did not say.

candidates.solves: Construction extraction often paraphrases or generalizes a speaker's explicit evaluative description (e.g., 'our team bond is awesome') into an abstract summary, losing the exact wording that future questions may ask for.

payload.name: Extract Object Descriptions from Referenced-Item Exchanges
payload.description: Use during extraction when one speaker asks about or comments on an object the other speaker just showed or mentioned, and the reply identifies or describes that object.
content: During extraction, when a speaker refers to an object with a demonstrative or pronoun ('this map', 'that picture', 'it') and the other speaker replies by identifying or describing the object, resolve the referent from the prior turn and create a candidate memory for the object and its description.

If the exchange shows the object was shown or shared, record an event memory with the sharer, the recipient, and the object identity; otherwise record a state memory for the owner/object only if ownership is explicit.
Do not require the object name to be repeated in the reply; use the preceding question or comment as context to identify the object.
Emit at most one memory per such exchange unless the reply states additional distinct facts about a different subject.

candidates.solves: Conversations where an object is shown or mentioned and then identified only in a reply to a follow-up question are missed because the subject is expressed by a demonstrative or pronoun. This skill makes extraction resolve the referent across turns so showing/sharing events and object descriptions are stored.

payload.name: Capture Explicit Rationale with Stated Opinions
payload.description: When a speaker states an opinion, belief, or preference and explicitly provides a reason or purpose, during extraction.
content: During extraction, when a speaker expresses an opinion, belief, or preference and explicitly states the reason or purpose (e.g., 'important to...', 'because...', 'so that...'), capture both the stance and the stated rationale in the same candidate.
Preserve the rationale verbatim enough to answer why-questions; do not reduce the candidate to only the stance.
Stop after capturing the stance and its explicitly stated rationale; do not infer unstated reasons or expand to other topics.

candidates.solves: This solves the problem of extraction candidates capturing only a speaker's stance or activity while dropping the explicitly stated reason or purpose, which later prevents answering why-questions about the speaker's beliefs.

payload.name: Preserve all explicitly listed experience elements
payload.description: Use during extraction when a message explicitly enumerates multiple distinct aspects that made an experience positive (e.g., relaxing, enjoyable, fun) and the memory should preserve each listed element.
content: During extraction, when a message explicitly lists multiple distinct elements of an experience (e.g., 'fresh air, peacefulness, and a cozy cabin made it a retreat'), preserve every stated element in the memory, including abstract qualities as well as concrete items.

Do not replace the enumeration with a single vague paraphrase or capture only the most concrete item; either create separate durable memories for each element or list all elements explicitly in one memory.
Stop after the explicitly stated elements are captured; do not infer additional aspects or expand into unrelated memories.

candidates.solves: When extraction collapses a message that explicitly lists multiple distinct reasons or elements that made an experience positive (enjoyable, relaxing, etc.) into a single vague paraphrase, it loses verifiable facts. This skill preserves each explicitly stated element so later evidence-based questions can be answered.

payload.name: Preserve All Explicit Preference Facets Before Duplicate Skip
payload.description: Use when a message states a preference or feeling with multiple explicit reasons or facets, or when a candidate is about to be SKIPped as a duplicate; preserve every explicit facet and only SKIP if the target memory already contains all of them.
content: During extraction, if a speaker gives multiple explicit reasons or facets for one preference, feeling, or state (e.g., emotional benefit plus practical benefit), include every explicitly stated facet in the candidate content; do not keep only the most prominent or emotional one.

During CRUD decisions, before SKIPping a candidate as 'duplicate information already represented', compare the candidate's explicit facts with the existing/updated memory. If the candidate contains any explicit facet not present in the target, do not SKIP it; create or update the memory to include that facet.
Capture only explicitly stated facets and stop; do not infer additional benefits or exhaustively expand the memory.

candidates.solves: Construction sometimes loses explicit preference details when a candidate captures only one facet of a multi-faceted statement and is then skipped as a duplicate even though the omitted facet is not stored anywhere. This skill ensures all explicitly stated facets are extracted and that duplicate SKIP decisions happen only when the target memory truly contains every candidate fact.

payload.name: Attribute Relational Views to Speaking User
payload.description: During extraction in multi-party conversations, if one speaker explicitly states a view about someone or something, attribute the memory to that speaker, not to the conversation partner who agrees or responds.
content: During extraction, when a speaker explicitly frames how they view someone or something (e.g., 'pets feel like family'), record the speaker as the subject of the memory, regardless of whether another participant expresses agreement or a similar view.
If two participants each state their own view, create separate memories for each speaker with their own subject; do not merge one speaker's statement into the other's existing memory.
Before attributing a relational statement to an existing memory, verify that the memory's subject matches the speaker of the message; if not, create a new memory for the correct speaker.
Stop after capturing each speaker's explicit view once per relationship; do not duplicate or expand with agreement phrases.

candidates.solves: Extraction in multi-party conversations sometimes attributes one speaker's explicit relational view to the other participant, causing facts to be stored under the wrong person. This skill ensures statements are attributed to the actual speaker, preventing cross-speaker contamination of relationship memories.

payload.name: Extract All Explicit Facts from a Message
payload.description: When a single message explicitly states multiple distinct durable facts (e.g., an event plus a peripheral detail), during extraction.
content: During extraction, when a message contains multiple distinct explicit facts (e.g., a speaker states they signed up for a class and also describes an incidental encounter), create a separate candidate for each distinct fact; do not let one salient detail suppress the other.
Identify the primary stated action, plan, or event and ensure it is captured, even if the message also contains a concrete or colorful peripheral detail.
Stop after all explicitly stated durable facts have been captured; do not add unstated inferences or duplicate candidates for the same fact.

candidates.solves: During extraction, when a user message explicitly states multiple distinct durable facts, the extractor may capture only the most salient or concrete detail and omit the primary action or plan, leading to missing memories. This skill ensures all explicitly stated facts, especially the primary event or plan, are captured in separate candidates without inventing unstated details.

payload.name: Extract Every Distinct Explicit Fact
payload.description: When a single message contains multiple distinct explicit facts and one fact is more salient or is the main topic, use this during extraction and CRUD.
content: During extraction, if a message states two or more independent explicit facts, create one candidate memory for each fact rather than a single candidate centered on the most salient topic.
Do not skip an explicit durable fact because it is mentioned in passing, as background, or in the same message as a more prominent topic; if it is clearly stated, extract it as its own candidate.
During CRUD, when adding or merging candidates, preserve all explicitly stated distinct facts; accepting a salient candidate must not cause other explicit facts to be dropped or overwritten.
Stop after capturing each distinct fact; do not infer unmentioned details or expand into related topics.

candidates.solves: Construction extraction sometimes records only the most salient statement from a message and omits other explicitly stated durable facts, leaving memory incomplete for later questions. This skill ensures each distinct explicit fact in a message becomes its own candidate and is preserved through CRUD.

payload.name: Resolve Pronoun References to Prior Entities
payload.description: Use during extraction when a message states a fact using a pronoun (it, this, that, they) that refers to an entity mentioned earlier in the conversation.
content: During extraction, when a message contains a pronoun (it, this, that, they) that refers to an entity explicitly mentioned earlier in the conversation, resolve the referent from the recent context and create a candidate memory for the stated fact about that entity, even if the entity name is not repeated.

If the stated fact includes a relative time phrase such as 'a year ago' or 'last month', resolve it against the message/session timestamp to an absolute year/date and record that in the memory content (e.g., bought/started in YYYY).
Choose the closest semantically matching antecedent when multiple candidates exist; if no clear referent exists, do not invent one and stop after extracting the fact.

candidates.solves: The construction agent sometimes skips a factual statement because the message uses a pronoun instead of repeating the entity name, so facts about previously mentioned pets, people, or objects are never stored even though the referent is clear from the conversation context.

payload.name: Extract Explicitly Stated Personal Values
payload.description: When a user explicitly says something is important to them, matters to them, or that they value it (e.g., 'X is important to me', 'I value X', 'X matters to me'), during extraction.
content: During extraction, when a user explicitly states a personal value or importance, create a separate durable preference or state candidate preserving that value in the user's own words, even if it is given as the reason for an activity.
If multiple distinct values are stated in one message, capture each value explicitly rather than absorbing them only into an event/activity memory.
During CRUD, when merging such a value into an existing memory, retain the explicit importance wording; do not replace it with only a description of the related activity.
Stop after capturing the stated values; do not infer additional values not explicitly mentioned.

candidates.solves: Extraction candidates often paraphrase a user's explicit statement of personal importance into an activity description, dropping the value itself (e.g., keeping the activity but losing that something is important to the user). This skill ensures explicitly stated values and importance are preserved as durable preference/state memories, so later questions asking why the user does something can be answered.

payload.name: Preserve Resolved Dates When Updating Event Memories
payload.description: When updating or enriching an existing event memory with a candidate that includes a relative time phrase, resolve the phrase to an absolute date and store it in both content and world_start.
content: When applying an UPDATE or MERGE to an existing event memory using a candidate with a relative time phrase, resolve the phrase against the message/session timestamp and write the absolute date (e.g., 2023-04-24) into the memory content and world_start.
Do not copy vague wording such as 'the previous day' or 'recently' into the updated content; the stored memory must stand alone without the source message.
If the existing memory already has a world_start, overwrite it with the resolved date for the new event unless the new event is a separate occurrence.
Stop after updating the single affected memory; do not propagate the date to unrelated memories.

candidates.solves: During memory updates, agents sometimes copy relative time phrases like 'yesterday' into the stored content and fail to carry over the correctly resolved absolute date, causing the fact's date to become ambiguous or lost. This skill prevents that by requiring the resolved absolute date to replace relative wording and update world_start whenever enriching an existing event memory.

payload.name: Preserve Explicit Event Timing in Extraction
payload.description: Use when a message states when an event, possession, or achievement happened using a relative or explicit time phrase, during extraction or memory update.
content: During extraction, if a message reports when an event, possession, or achievement occurred (e.g., 'a few years ago', 'last summer', 'in 2021'), include that time phrase explicitly in the candidate content.
Do not replace the stated time with the message/session date; keep the speaker's wording so future questions about timing can be answered.
Also apply when updating an existing memory that later gains an explicit time qualifier.
Stop at the stated time; do not compute or infer an exact date unless the speaker supplies one.

candidates.solves: Extraction sometimes keeps the descriptive or emotional details of an event or possession but drops explicit temporal qualifiers such as 'a few years ago', so later questions about when it happened cannot be answered. This skill ensures that explicit timing stated in the source is preserved in the extracted memory.

payload.name: Extract distinct facts alongside relative time expressions
payload.description: When a message contains a relative time expression plus other factual claims such as counts, attendance, or outcomes, extract each distinct fact as its own memory candidate during construction.
content: During extraction, treat each message as a bundle of distinct factual claims: numeric quantities, event details, stated preferences, and relative time expressions each belong in their own candidate.

When a message mixes a relative time expression with another fact (e.g., '7 people attended' and 'want to do it again next month'), resolve the time expression for the relevant candidate and still create a separate candidate for the other fact.
Do not let applying a time-resolution skill suppress extraction of the remaining substantive facts in the same message.
Stop after each distinct fact is captured once; do not add extra candidates for paraphrases or inferred details.

candidates.solves: Construction sometimes only resolves a relative time expression and fails to extract other explicit facts in the same message (e.g., attendance counts, outcomes). This skill ensures each distinct claim in a message becomes its own memory candidate.

payload.name: Preserve Cumulative Counts of Repeated Events
payload.description: When a message reports another occurrence in a series of discrete events for the same person (e.g., a second, fourth, or latest win/milestone), use this guidance.
content: During extraction, when a speaker reports a repeated discrete event with an ordinal or 'another' (e.g., second tournament win, another visit), include the ordinal/cumulative count in the candidate content; do not store only the latest occurrence.

During CRUD, before updating an existing memory with a new occurrence of the same event type for the same subject, search the pool for prior occurrences; preserve the earlier occurrence(s) instead of overwriting their content and date.
If prior occurrences exist, write a compact count memory or add the cumulative total to the updated memory so the number of occurrences is explicit (e.g., 'has now won N tournaments').
Stop once the cumulative count is recorded; do not enumerate every occurrence or aggregate different event types.

candidates.solves: Construction agents sometimes UPDATE an existing event memory with a newer occurrence of the same kind, overwriting earlier facts and losing the ability to answer count questions. This skill ensures repeated discrete events are preserved and their cumulative count is made explicit.

payload.name: Resolve Relative Time in Extracted Memories
payload.description: When extracting or updating an event/state memory from a statement containing a relative time expression (e.g., 'last month', 'last Friday', 'next month'), resolve it from the message timestamp and record the absolute date.
content: During extraction, if a statement contains a relative time expression (e.g., 'last month', 'last Friday', 'next month'), resolve it to an absolute calendar date or month using the message/session timestamp.

Include the resolved absolute time explicitly in the memory content (e.g., 'lost his job in October 2023'), not just a relative phrase like 'last month'; align world_start/world_end with the resolved date.
When updating an existing memory, preserve the same absolute anchor and add the newly resolved timing if missing.
Stop after anchoring the stated time; do not infer further dates or expand the memory with additional unstated details.

candidates.solves: Construction extraction sometimes stores relative time expressions verbatim without anchoring them to the message timestamp, so later questions about when an event happened cannot be answered from the memory. This skill ensures relative time references in extracted event/state memories are resolved to absolute dates and recorded explicitly.

payload.name: Resolve Relative Time in Event Extraction
payload.description: When extracting an event memory from a message that contains a relative time expression such as 'last summer', 'yesterday', or 'two weeks ago', resolve it to an absolute date from the message timestamp instead of using the message date.
content: During extraction, when a message describes an event with a relative time expression (e.g., 'last summer', 'yesterday', 'two weeks ago'), resolve it to an absolute date using the message/session timestamp and set the event memory's world_start (and world_end if bounded) to that resolved date, not the message date.
Include the resolved time in the candidate content (e.g., 'in summer 2022') so the timing remains searchable; do not leave only vague phrasing such as 'during her vacation'.
Stop after capturing the event and its resolved timing; do not expand into additional memories unless the message contains other distinct facts.

candidates.solves: Extraction often drops relative time references in event statements and defaults event dates to the message timestamp, so later questions about when something happened cannot be answered. This skill makes extractors resolve relative temporal expressions to absolute dates and store them with the event memory.

payload.name: Resolve Relative Event Start Dates
payload.description: During extraction, when a message describes an event or state start with a relative time phrase (e.g., 'a few days ago', 'last week', 'recently'), apply this guidance to set the correct world_start.
content: When a message describes an event or state start with a relative time phrase (e.g., 'a few days ago', 'last month', 'recently'), resolve the start date from the message/session timestamp by subtracting the indicated duration; never use the message date as the event start unless the phrase explicitly says 'today' or 'now'.
For vague phrases like 'a few days ago', record an approximate earlier date in world_start and preserve the original relative wording in memory content so the uncertainty remains traceable.
Keep this resolution consistent across extraction and any later ADD/UPDATE/MERGE; do not drop the relative expression in favor of an overly precise date.

candidates.solves: When extracting the start date of an event or state from a message that uses a relative time expression (e.g., 'a few days ago', 'last week'), the agent incorrectly sets the event's world_start to the message timestamp, losing the temporal offset. This skill teaches the agent to resolve the relative expression against the message/session timestamp and preserve the nuance.

payload.name: Extract Past Event Times from Relative Phrases
payload.description: When a message states an event happened a relative time ago (e.g., 'a year ago', 'last week', 'two days ago'), extract it with an absolute date.
content: During extraction, when a message contains a relative past-time phrase (e.g., 'a year ago', 'last month', 'last week', 'two days ago') attached to an event, purchase, action, or change in state, create an event or state candidate for that fact and resolve the phrase to an approximate absolute date/time using the message/session timestamp.
Include the resolved absolute time (e.g., 'bought X in January 2022') in the memory content or world_start rather than storing only the relative phrase.
If the exact day is unknown, record the best known precision (year, month, or date) and do not infer extra details beyond the stated event; stop after capturing the event and its time.

candidates.solves: Construction agents sometimes skip statements that describe when a past event occurred using relative time phrases (e.g., 'a year ago', 'last week'), leaving no memory for future temporal queries. This skill ensures such relative past times are resolved to absolute dates and stored with the event.
